text: Welcome. Today’s lecture is about what happens when a workflow stops being immediate and starts happening in the background. The business goal may look the same, but the engineering problem changes a lot once work moves across time. Now correctness depends on events, queues, workers, retries, ordering, and whether we can actually observe what happened. The key question is: what has to become explicit so the system still behaves correctly under pressure?

Imagine you take a synchronous operation and offload it to a background worker so the user gets a faster response. That is usually a good move for responsiveness, but it also means the original method no longer guarantees immediate completion. The work may be delayed, repeated, or processed in a different order. So the design has changed, even if the business story sounds unchanged. The real challenge is making the hidden assumptions visible before the system is trusted.

This topic breaks into five connected ideas. An event names what happened. A queue stores work until it can be handled. A worker performs the work. Evidence tells us whether the behavior was actually correct. And design choice is where we decide how to protect the important invariant. The important engineering habit here is to connect the abstraction to proof, not just to implementation.

An event is a record of something that already happened. That sounds simple, but it matters because past occurrences are not the same as current state. A common mistake is to treat an event like a method call and assume the rest of the system will immediately agree. In practice, the event becomes useful only if it is observable and tied to the invariant we care about. If we ignore that, the code may look fine on the happy path while still producing duplicate work or stale decisions under pressure.

A queue is the buffer that lets work wait until a consumer is ready. That buffering is exactly what makes it useful, and also what introduces risk. The producer can move on while the consumer is delayed, retried, or temporarily unavailable. So the queue is not just a convenience layer; it is part of the system’s timing model. When you use it, you need to think about delivery, ordering, and what evidence proves that an item was handled correctly.

The worker is the component that pulls work from the queue and does something real, usually a side effect like shipping an order, cleaning a file, or sending a notification. This is where correctness can fail in a very concrete way. The worker may run more than once, crash halfway through, or acknowledge completion too late. So the worker logic has to be built around the idea that delivery and execution are not the same thing.

Decoupling means the producer does not need to know who is consuming the event, or whether that consumer is even online right now. That is a strength because it reduces direct dependency and improves responsiveness. But it also means the producer can no longer assume immediate completion. The real design question becomes whether the system can still protect its invariant when the two sides are separated in time and ownership.

An asynchronous boundary is the point where work continues later, often on another worker or event loop. That boundary is where hidden assumptions become dangerous. Once you cross it, retries become possible, timing changes, and evidence matters much more. A common mistake is to think of the code as one continuous flow when in reality it has become a sequence of partially independent steps. That is why we need logs, IDs, and repeatable tests.

Here the important idea is that event processing is really a state machine. The work begins enqueued, gets delivered, enters processing, finishes as completed, and is only then acknowledged. If the worker crashes before completion, the item may move into retry pending and come back later. The invariant we care about is simple to say but hard to preserve: each external side effect should happen at most once, even if the queue delivers the same event more than once. That is the property the state model is trying to protect.

Let’s make the failure concrete. Worker A ships order-42 and then crashes before it can acknowledge the message. The queue assumes the delivery was not completed and redelivers the same event to Worker B. Now the system can ship the same order again, or at least produce logs that no longer line up with the actual outcome. This is uncomfortable because the baseline version often looks correct until exactly this kind of timing pressure appears. The evidence students should capture here is the delivery ID, the worker logs, and the side-effect trail that proves the duplicate path happened.

The pressure here is at-least-once delivery combined with an acknowledgement timeout and a worker restart. Each part is reasonable on its own, but together they expose the hidden assumption that delivery count equals execution count. That assumption is false. The result can be duplicate side effects, missing notifications, or a run that never reaches a clean final acknowledgement. The key lesson is that the consumer must be designed around uncertainty, not around the fantasy of exactly-once execution.

The protected property is that retried events do not inflate side effects or hide lost work. To defend that property, we use idempotency keys, durable completion records, retry-safe handlers, and reconciliation scans. Those controls make invalid repeats visible or harmless. But they are not free. They add storage, more state to reason about, and more complex handler logic. That trade-off is worth naming explicitly, because a fix that works only by making the system opaque is not a real fix.

This lecture is really about evidence as much as it is about architecture. A defensible claim needs delivery IDs, operation IDs, worker logs, and an audit trail that ties the action to the outcome. If the worker succeeds but the acknowledgement is lost, the evidence still needs to explain what happened. That is why we design for delivery uncertainty and then prove the result with structured records. In an Integrity Packet, this is the material that supports the design decision.

There are several ways to respond, and each one trades simplicity for control. A simple baseline is easiest to explain, but it often hides timing assumptions. A guarded state transition protects the invariant directly, but it requires careful state modeling. Explicit coordination makes dependencies visible, though it can create waiting or bottlenecks. An idempotent design is especially useful for queues and retries, but it needs keys and deduplication logic. The main takeaway is that the mechanism should match the failure, not just the framework you happen to be using.

For practice, start by identifying the invariant or progress property that matters most in your own system. Then write one normal scenario that should succeed and one pressure scenario that could expose the failure. Before you run the pressure case, add operation IDs and entity IDs to your logs so the behavior can be traced. If you apply a fix, capture before and after evidence. And finally, update the Integrity Packet with the assumption, the evidence, the validation, and any remaining risk.

This lecture connects directly to A3. You should be able to point to a real object, workflow, event, failure, or recovery mechanism in your own project and explain how it behaves under pressure. The goal is not just to say that you use queues or background work, but to defend the design with runnable commands, structured logs, before and after behavior, diagrams, and failure reproduction. That is the level of evidence expected in the oral defense and in the Integrity Packet.
